This merge runs without a single warning. Four orders go in, and six come out. Revenue was two hundred sixty-five. Now it's three hundred seventy-five, and nothing on the screen says why. The pandas round is full of code like that: it runs, and it's wrong. There are fourteen questions. Nine are worked on real frames, in pandas three, and five go quickly at the end. The merge comes back at question six. First, why nobody wants to see a loop.

Question one. Why is vectorization preferred over Python loops? Here are five prices and quantities. The loop walks the rows one at a time, multiplying in Python. The vectorized line hands both whole columns to NumPy, which multiplies them in compiled code, in one call. The revenues are the same. On a million rows, timed in WebAssembly, the way this page runs Python, the loop takes several hundred milliseconds. The vectorized line takes about one millisecond. That's hundreds of times faster. Write a loop only when no vectorized version exists. Next, the pattern under every groupby.

Question two. What is split, apply, combine, and what does groupby return? Split sorts the rows into one group per region. Apply runs a function on each group, here a sum. Combine puts the answers together: East fifty, North two forty, South one fifty. On its own, groupby returns a data frame group by object, and nothing is aggregated yet. Sum one column, and you get a Series, indexed by region. Name several aggregates in ag, and you get a data frame. Either way, the regions are the index until you reset it.
